0f2aa71ad8b0b90c: PETALING JAYA: Beberapa inisiatif untuk memperkasakan ekonomi Bumiputera seperti diumumkan dalam Belanjawan 2027 perlu disusuli dengan penyelarasan akses lebih berkesan bagi memastikan usahawan tidak terlepas dan tercicir daripada peluang serta kemudahan disediakan.

Presiden Persatuan Pedagang dan Pengusaha Melayu Malaysia (Perdasama), Azamanizam Baharon, berkata ia kerana isu kesukaran mendapatkan akses kepada pembiayaan, peluang kontrak dan kemudahan bagi usahawan perusahaan mikro, kecil dan sederhana (PMKS) Bumiputera masih berbangkit meskipun tiga kitaran belanjawan telah berlalu.
"Kita menyambut baik dengan pengumuman oleh Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim khususnya komitmen kerajaan dalam memperkukuh agenda pembangunan dan pemerkasaan ekonomi Bumiputera.
"Namun, kita berpandangan kejayaan sesebuah belanjawan tidak seharusnya diukur berdasarkan jumlah semata-mata tetapi sejauh mana ia boleh diakses.

"Ini kerana persoalan sama masih berbangkit dalam kalangan usahawan Bumiputera meskipun tiga kitaran belanjawan telah berlalu. Ia melibatkan kesukaran mendapatkan akses kepada pembiayaan, peluang kontrak dan pelbagai kemudahan yang diwujudkan," katanya dalam kenyataan.

Justeru katanya, beliau berkata kerajaan wajar mempertimbangkan satu mekanisme untuk menyelaras akses terhadap insiatif diwujudkan menerusi penglibatan persatuan perniagaan yang mempunyai jaringan langsung dengan usahawan di lapangan.
"Mekanisme ini perlu menumpukan tiga perkara utama iaitu akses jelas dan bersasar selain pemantauan dan akauntabiliti termasuk pengukuran impak sebenar.

"Setiap inisiatif perlu disertakan dengan panduan kelayakan, dokumen diperlukan, saluran permohonan, pegawai atau pusat rujukan serta jangka masa pemprosesan yang munasabah. Pemohon juga wajar menerima pengesahan penerimaan, maklumat status dan penjelasan yang sewajarnya sekiranya permohonan tidak diluluskan," katanya.

Menerusi pembentangan Belanjawan 2027 pada Jumaat lalu, Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim mengumumkan beberapa inisiatif untuk memperkasa ekonomi Bumiputera termasuk menaikkan perolehan kerajaan untuk kontraktor Bumiputera G1-G4 dinaikkan kepada RM7.5 bilion, berbanding RM4 bilion tahun ini, penyediaan pembiayaan dana Teraju sehingga RM1 bilion dan menaikkan pembiayaan Perbadanan Usahawan Nasional Berhad kepada RM500 juta.

Selain itu, inisiatif itu juga membabitkan sasaran perolehan syarikat berkaitan kerajaan (GLC) dan Petronas RM58 bilion daripada syarikat Bumiputera serta Dana Ciptawan bernilai RM250 juta yang diwujudkan untuk membantu pertumbuhan syarikat sederhana Bumiputera.

Selain itu, Azamanizam berkata pihaknya juga menggesa kementerian, jabatan, institusi kewangan serta kira-kira 80 agensi yang terlibat dalam pembangunan Bumiputera untuk berperanan lebih proaktif dan responsif mengikut keperluan sebenar usahawan.
Katanya, kesukaran mendapatkan akses pembiayaan perlu ditangani dengan serius menerusi sokongan lebih telus dan berkesan.

"Usahawan ini ialah golongan yang berusaha membayar gaji pekerja, menanggung kos operasi, mendapatkan pelanggan, membayar komitmen pembiayaan dan memastikan perniagaan terus bertahan dalam persekitaran yang semakin mencabar.
"Apabila akses kepada bantuan dan pembiayaan yang sewajarnya sukar diperoleh, sebahagian usahawan mungkin terpaksa mencari sumber pembiayaan alternatif yang lebih mahal atau berisiko," katanya.
d6a67abbda1a3628: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 11 — K-pop girl group TWICE’s plans for a small-scale fan party marking their 11th anniversary have reportedly drawn criticism from some fans, amid continuing questions over the members’ future with JYP Entertainment.
US-based K-pop news site allkpop reported that the ONCE UPON A THRI11 fan party will be held in Seoul on October 17, with only 750 places available across three sessions.
Each session, scheduled for 2pm, 4pm and 6pm, will accommodate 250 fans, while the exact venue will reportedly be disclosed only to those selected to attend.
The limited capacity has reportedly prompted complaints from fans, given TWICE’s international following and the larger venues used for previous anniversary celebrations, according to the report.
The group previously held its eighth- and ninth-anniversary events at Seoul’s Olympic Hall, before staging its 10th-anniversary fan meeting at Hwajeong Gymnasium.

The upcoming celebration also comes amid reported uncertainty over the nine members’ individual contracts with JYP Entertainment, after all of them renewed their agreements with the agency in July 2022.

Jeongyeon reportedly left JYP in August and signed with Varo Entertainment to pursue acting while remaining a member of TWICE, while Chaeyoung has also been reported to be pursuing separate arrangements for her individual activities while continuing with the group.
allkpop said uncertainty over the other members’ individual arrangements has added to fan interest in whether the group will address its future during the anniversary gathering.
TWICE debuted under JYP Entertainment in October 2015 and has since grown into one of K-pop’s most prominent girl groups.
6aef9a8a72ca8751: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 11 — Two men suspected of stealing cables were arrested after the car they were travelling in crashed into a drain while fleeing from police in Taman Sri Watan, Ampang, yesterday.
Ampang Jaya police chief ACP Khairul Anuar Khalid said police received a tip-off from the public at about 5.53am.

He said a police patrol spotted a blue Perodua Aruz without registration plates parked by Jalan Watan 8. The driver attempted to flee when police arrived, prompting a chase that ended when the car crashed into a drain.
“Both men in the vehicle were arrested,” he said in a statement today.
The case is being investigated under Sections 186, 379, 431A and 124K of the Penal Code, as well as Section 235 of the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998.
Earlier, two videos showing police arresting the suspects behind a row of shops went viral on Threads. The videos also showed cables believed to have been targeted for theft. — Bernama
5aa3221891cf9de8: MELBOURNE: Two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge won his first marathon in three years on Sunday when the Kenyan great cruised to victory at Melbourne.
The most-decorated marathoner in history crossed the finish line in 2hrs 9min 10sec, two seconds inside the race record.
It was his first victory over the distance since Berlin in 2023 and part of his "World Tour" to raise funds for causes he believes in.
The 41-year-old former world record-holder announced in 2025 he planned to complete marathons on all seven continents, including Antarctica, over two years.
Melbourne was the third stop after South Africa and Brazil.
He broke away inside the last 10km on a course raced partly on the Australian Formula One track at Albert Park and which finished inside the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground.
"On the course, it was really wonderful, I enjoyed seeing people standing, cheering, and shouting my name," Kipchoge said, looking fresh at the finish.
He would have gone faster, but slowed down inside the MCG waving to fans.
"It was actually different -- running on a beautiful course, but also running on the Formula One track, and above all else, finishing on a cricket ground," he added.
"It makes me proud to run with the younger generation and inspire the running community in Melbourne."
Australian Thomas Do Canto was runner-up in 2:10:35 while New Zealand's Camille French came first in the women's race in 2:28:25.
1badde5af53d1181: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 11 — A total of 15 areas nationwide recorded unhealthy Air Pollutant Index (API) readings as of 9am today, with Pasir Gudang, Johor, recording the highest reading at 180.

According to the Department of Environment’s (DOE) Air Pollutant Index Management System (APIMS) portal, seven other areas in Johor also recorded unhealthy API readings: Larkin (178), Kota Tinggi (166), Tangkak (164), Segamat (162), Pengerang (160), Kluang (159) and Batu Pahat (151), national news agency Bernama reported.
In Pahang, Balok Baru in Kuantan recorded an API reading of 159, while Rompin recorded 53 and Cheras in Kuala Lumpur registered 157.
Other areas with unhealthy API readings were Kemaman and Kuala Terengganu in Terengganu, which recorded 156 each, while Paka registered 133 and Alor Gajah in Melaka recorded 103.
Meanwhile, 50 areas recorded moderate API readings, while three recorded good air quality.
API readings of zero to 50 indicate good air quality, 51 to 100 moderate, 101 to 200 unhealthy, 201 to 300 very unhealthy, and readings above 300 hazardous.
6214220fd8c1c463: MIAMI: Lionel Messi scored twice to help Inter Miami rout DC United 4-0 on Saturday, taking a victory in his first match since saying farewell to the Argentina national team.

Four nights after scoring in his final match for the Albiceleste in a victory over Benin, the 39-year-old South American superstar struck in the 47th and 60th minutes as defending MLS champions Miami won for only the second time in their past 11 league matches.
A first-half brace by Luis Suarez staked the Herons to the lead as they improved to 13-5 with 10 drawn for 49 points, jumping from third to second in the Eastern Conference.
Messi hopes to make Miami the first team to win back-to-back MLS crowns since the Los Angeles Galaxy in 2011-12.
Messi, the top point producer in the league with 23 goals plus assists on 13 others, seeks a third consecutive MLS Most Valuable Player award.
Uruguayan striker Suarez scored in the third minute to give Miami the lead, blasting a left-footed shot from the heart of the box into the top left corner.
Suarez struck again in the 39th for his 16th goal of the campaign, assisted like his first of the night by German Berterame.
Messi blasted home a left-footed shot off an assist from Suarez to give Miami a 3-0 lead and evaded three defenders to add another goal 13 minutes later as the pink-clad hosts pulled away to stay.
In other games, Scottish striker Lewis Morgan and American Djordje Mihailovic scored in second-half stoppage time to rally Toronto for a 2-1 home victory over Montreal.
The visitors grabbed the lead in the Canadian clash on a goal by Mexican forward Daniel Rios in the 52nd minute.
Toronto, however, battled back for the equalizer by winger Morgan, obtained last month from San Diego, in the third minute of stoppage time, his first regular-season MLS goal in two years.
Former Montreal standout Mihailovic struck for the decider in the fifth minute of extra time.
"Now I've scored on both sides of this derby," he said. "It feels good."
Toronto snapped a three-game losing streak to pull within a point of an East playoff berth.
At Chicago, Swiss forward Maren Haile-Selassie scored in the 87th minute to give the 10-man Chicago Fire a 2-1 triumph over New York City.
Austrian midfielder Hannes Wolf gave City the lead in the 19th minute and Chicago dropped to 10 men when Ivory coast midfielder Dje D'Avilla received his second yellow card in the 43rd minute.
Swede Anton Saletros equalized for Chicago in the 55th minute, setting the stage for the decider.
7429477c52a80dba: KOTA KINABALU, Oct 11 — A special tax deduction incentive for the Ihsan Food Bank Initiative (i-FB) under Budget 2027 is expected to encourage greater participation by strategic partners, including the corporate sector, in strengthening the food bank ecosystem.

Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Minister Datuk Armizan Mohd Ali said the government had agreed to grant special tax deductions to parties contributing food and equipment for the i-FB initiative from January 1 next year until December 31, 2030.

He said his ministry appreciated Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim and the Finance Ministry for accepting its proposal to support the implementation of i-FB, one of 44 tax incentive measures announced under Budget 2027.

“This tax incentive is in line with efforts to strengthen the food bank ecosystem through integrated coordination that opens the door as widely as possible to participation by various parties,” he told a press conference before attending the Universiti Malaysia Sabah (UMS) Alumni Homecoming & Fundraising Dinner 2026, last night.

According to him, the special tax deduction introduced serves as an incentive and recognition to broaden the participation of strategic partners, including through contributions of food, equipment and operational support needed to strengthen the implementation of i-FB.
Armizan said the detailed mechanism for implementing the special tax deduction incentive for i-FB would be coordinated with the Finance Ministry.

He added that collaboration with strategic partners, including the corporate sector and voluntary organisations, would enable i-FB to drive collective efforts to ease the cost-of-living burden on those in need, rescue food from waste and protect the environment.

Meanwhile, at the dinner, i-FB grants were also presented to the UMS Student Consumer Movement, which will coordinate the initiative at their respective educational institutions and within local communities.
Armizan said the initial grants would be used to provide equipment and dedicated i-FB spaces on campuses to facilitate the receipt, storage and distribution of donated food to students in need.
“This initiative also creates opportunities for contributions from various parties to help ease the cost of living among students,” he said.

The i-FB initiative is one of the cost-of-living assistance measures implemented nationwide, with the Cost of Living Division of the Ministry of Domestic Trade and Cost of Living serving as its secretariat and aiming to secure participation from government agencies, the private sector, non-governmental organisations and individuals. — Bernama
9e8617f1cd440107: OCTOBER 11 — The conventional wisdom that China's economic slowdown necessarily signals its strategic decline deserves serious reconsideration.

Indeed, the assumption that India, Vietnam or other emerging economies can readily replace China as the world's manufacturing powerhouse may be one of the most consequential misjudgements in contemporary geopolitics.

This is the central argument of The Next China Is Still China: An Insider's Playbook for Winning in the New Era, co-authored by Joe Ngai and Nick Leung, two senior figures associated with McKinsey's extensive engagement with China's economic transformation.
Their book offers an important corrective to the increasingly fashionable narrative that China has reached the limits of its economic potential.

Rather than treating China as an exhausted growth story, Ngai and Leung contend that the country is entering another phase of economic transformation, one driven less by inexpensive labour and infrastructure expansion than by technological innovation, industrial sophistication and intense domestic competition.
Their argument deserves close attention, especially in Southeast Asia.
For more than four decades, China's economic rise was associated with manufacturing, exports, urbanisation and an extraordinary capacity to mobilise capital and labour.
That model transformed China into the world's second-largest economy and created industrial ecosystems of unprecedented complexity.
Yet the authors suggest that China's next economic chapter cannot be understood through the assumptions of its previous development model.
China is increasingly competing in electric vehicles, advanced batteries, robotics, artificial intelligence and sophisticated manufacturing technologies.
Its companies are no longer merely producing goods designed elsewhere.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

The author argues that China’s slower growth does not necessarily mean strategic decline, and that Asean should strengthen its own technological and industrial capabilities while recognising its continued deep economic integration with China. — AFP pic
They are developing technologies, establishing industrial standards and competing internationally on quality, speed and cost.
One particularly compelling aspect of the book concerns the intensity of domestic competition.
Ngai and Leung portray China as an exceptionally demanding environment in which companies must continuously improve their products and operations simply to survive.
Chinese consumers are increasingly sophisticated, digitally connected and willing to switch brands.
Consequently, domestic competition has become a powerful mechanism for technological adaptation.
Companies that survive such an environment may emerge internationally stronger, more efficient and more innovative.
This argument is persuasive, although it requires qualification.
Intense competition can certainly stimulate innovation.
But excessive competition can also undermine profitability, encourage overcapacity and produce destructive price wars.
China's extraordinary industrial capabilities therefore do not automatically guarantee sustainable economic returns.
The distinction between industrial strength and economic sustainability remains essential.
Another major contribution of the book lies in challenging the proposition that the next China will necessarily emerge somewhere outside China.
India possesses demographic advantages and a growing industrial base.
Vietnam has become an important manufacturing destination. Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia are attracting investments in semiconductors, electric vehicles and digital infrastructure.
Nevertheless, none individually possesses China's complete combination of industrial scale, supplier networks, infrastructure, engineering capabilities and domestic market depth.
Indeed, much of the manufacturing diversification taking place across Asean remains connected to Chinese intermediate goods, machinery, investment and technological expertise.
This creates an important geopolitical paradox.
Companies seeking to reduce their dependence on China may discover that their new production facilities elsewhere remain dependent on Chinese supply chains.
Diversification does not necessarily amount to decoupling.
For Asean, this distinction is strategically significant.
The region should welcome investments relocating from China while recognising that the resulting economic networks may continue to be deeply integrated with Chinese industrial capabilities.
Asean must therefore avoid the temptation to interpret every new factory established in Southeast Asia as evidence of China's economic retreat.
In many cases, such investments represent the international expansion of China's industrial ecosystem rather than its displacement.
The book is equally valuable for its implications concerning American strategic competition with China.
Washington has increasingly emphasised technological restrictions, industrial policy and supply-chain resilience.
Yet China's economic importance cannot simply be legislated out of existence.
Even as geopolitical tensions intensify, the economic interdependence between China, the United States and Asean remains substantial.
This does not mean that China's rise is irreversible.
The authors' generally optimistic interpretation must be balanced against serious structural difficulties.
China faces demographic ageing, property-sector weaknesses, local government indebtedness, subdued domestic demand and growing resistance to its overseas commercial expansion.
Technological progress alone cannot resolve all these challenges.
Nor can industrial dominance substitute indefinitely for stronger household consumption and sustainable productivity growth.
Nevertheless, the book's essential contribution is to demonstrate why these difficulties should not be confused with an inevitable collapse of Chinese economic power.
For Asean, the appropriate response is neither uncritical enthusiasm nor excessive apprehension.
Instead, Asean must become more strategically sophisticated.
The Asean Outlook on the Indo-Pacific provides a useful foundation for maintaining openness, inclusivity and cooperation amid intensifying major-power competition.
But diplomatic principles must be accompanied by technological investment, stronger regional supply chains and the development of indigenous capabilities.
Asean's circumscribed power means that it cannot individually or collectively match China's industrial scale.
Yet it can strengthen its bargaining position through economic integration, institutional cooperation and strategic diversification.
Malaysia, particularly as an important semiconductor and electrical and electronics manufacturing hub, has much to gain from understanding these transformations.
The challenge is to move beyond assembly and investment attraction towards research, innovation, advanced engineering and technological ownership.
Ultimately, Ngai and Leung have produced a timely and provocative contribution to the debate over China's economic future.
Their central proposition is convincing precisely because it rejects the simplistic assumption that slower growth necessarily means diminishing relevance.
The next China may be older, slower-growing and confronted by formidable geopolitical constraints.
But it may also be more technologically sophisticated, industrially competitive and internationally embedded.
For Asean, the lesson is unmistakable.
China's transformation is not a development to be observed from a distance.
It is a structural change that will directly influence Southeast Asia's economic opportunities, strategic autonomy and geopolitical future.
Understanding the next China is therefore inseparable from understanding the next Asean.
* Phar Kim Beng is professor of Asean Studies, and director at the Institute of International and Asean Studies, International Islamic University Malaysia.
** This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
828593d1a5b5ab85: GEORGE TOWN, Oct 11 — Penang is ready to work with the federal government to establish the National Integrated Care Centres of Excellence (NICE) in the state as part of efforts to prepare for an ageing population.

Chief Minister Chow Kon Yeow said the state government would cooperate in implementing the initiative, announced in Budget 2027 yesterday, which aims to provide training, research and care facilities for the elderly.

He said the State Economic Planning Division (BPEN) would be asked to liaise with the relevant ministries to obtain details of the proposed development, as information on its location and implementation in Penang was not yet available.

“We certainly welcome it and the state government will provide cooperation to ensure this facility can be established in Penang,” he told reporters after officiating the second State Heritage Declaration Ceremony under the Penang State Heritage Enactment 2011 for 2026 here yesterday.

Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim announced when tabling Budget 2027 yesterday that two NICE facilities would be developed in Penang and Sarawak to provide training, research and elderly care as the country prepares for an ageing population.
Chow said the growing number of senior citizens required targeted policies and programmes to ensure their welfare and needs were addressed effectively.

He said Penang was expected to become an ageing state in the next few years, adding that addressing the associated challenges required not only government action but also the involvement of the private sector and the community.

“The state government, the private sector and the community must all take the ageing process and the status of an ageing state seriously. This requires policies, infrastructure, care homes for the elderly, awareness programmes, welfare support and so on,” he said.

In a separate development, Chow said the state government would seek further information on the proposed 122-acre NCT InnoSphere development involving Penang and Kulim, Kedah, which was also announced in Budget 2027.

Anwar said NCT InnoSphere would be developed as a heavy vehicle, engineering, maintenance and logistics hub to support industries in Kulim and Penang under efforts to further strengthen the Special Border Economic Zone (SBEZ). — Bernama
80bb1834c8e5d564: NORTH JACKSON: For Doug Rende, who runs an aluminum product manufacturer in the US state of Ohio, president Donald Trump's tariffs have meant millions of dollars more in annual costs -- and recently, the Iran war has made shipments even more expensive.
Rende is chief executive at Shapes Unlimited, one of many American producers smarting from Trump's economic policies as midterm elections approach.
"Frustrating would be one word," Rende told AFP.
"And I think that we're sensing a lack of trust in not only the administration but the governmental process, the role of Congress to rein in executive power," he added.
Since returning to the presidency in January 2025, Trump has wielded executive authority to slap tariffs on various products and countries.
Besides aluminum, the duties hit steel and autos too, while US trading partners face additional tariffs that vary by country.
Even as some American manufacturers have benefited as their foreign competitors encounter higher barriers, others struggle with ballooning costs and persistent uncertainty.
Trump's spiraling trade fight with Canada and war with Iran have only deepened worries.
Grievances over Trump's trade policies are among fault lines that Democrats hope will work in their favor as they push to flip control of the Senate and House of Representatives in November's vote.
Tough to cope
Rende's company in North Jackson, Ohio, makes and distributes aluminum building products used in fixtures like fences.
Trump's tariffs on aluminum have steadily climbed, from 10 percent during his first presidency to 25% and then 50% last year, and Rende has felt the impact.
"This year alone, it's upwards of US$4.5 million to US$5 million in additional costs," Rende said.
"There's only so much that the end consumer is willing to eat," he added. "So, we absorb a healthy portion."
These added costs include steeper transportation fees, as fuel prices surged with the US-Israel war on Iran. Surcharges are "upwards of $6,500 per container" of goods from suppliers, Rende said.
As a result, he has paused recruitment for new jobs while investing in more robotic assembly.

Sam Miller, another Ohio manufacturer who makes kitchen and bathroom products, has been hit on both fronts in Trump's trade wars, paying tariffs on imported materials from Asia while finding it harder to expand into Canada because of trade tensions.

"It's been difficult for businesses to manage," Miller told AFP from his factory floor in Warren as a machine hummed nearby, cutting countertop material. "I do think that there will be a shift away from Republican views."
Although Miller received refunds after the Supreme Court struck down many of Trump's duties, the US leader has since reinstated many of them.
'Straining'
Deteriorating US-Canada ties add to his challenges, with Washington and Ottawa slapping tariffs on each other's products after trade negotiations collapsed in August.
"We're selling into Canada and it is particularly straining on both us and our customers," Miller said.
He originally planned on opening a distribution facility in Canada this year, but progress has slowed.
Guy Coviello, president of the Youngstown Warren Regional Chamber, told AFP he is monitoring tariffs, the Iran war and immigration very closely.
These are a "mixed bag" for firms but negative overall, said Coviello, whose business group has some 3,000 members.
Some firms have lost customers or had to downsize, he said.
Canada is also Ohio's biggest export market, with a third of Ohio's exports going to the country.
"Where it gets even more complicated is that there are some goods that go back and forth across the border multiple times," he said.
The Iran war adds to stresses, raising freight costs and hitting aluminum supplies due to drone attacks in the Middle East.
With a lack of new US aluminum smelters, Coviello said: "We are all for tariffs for critical items such as defense and medical industry."
But he added: "We have to be careful when you're talking about products that are not crucial and are not available in the US."
c142d89c27fa3b30: PENSACOLA: Four people died in the southeastern United States as post-tropical cyclone Isaias threatened flooding and tornado risks Saturday as it moved northward after making landfall on Florida's Gulf Coast.

Isaias roared ashore late Friday as a Category 2 hurricane near the resort community of Destin, packing sustained winds of 165 kph before weakening overnight, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) said.
It was the first hurricane of an Atlantic season tamed by a historic El Nino weather phenomenon, and the first hurricane since 2024 to hit the US mainland.
In Mary Esther, a coastal community near Destin, Matt Howard said he was fortunate the storm weakened ahead of landfall.
Despite losing power and having his neighbor's metal shed crash into his backyard, "overall, we were okay," he told AFP.
"We hunkered down, got in the center of our house, and did all the things you're supposed to do, and luckily came out on the other side," he said.
Officials reported at least four deaths related to the storm, including two from trees falling on homes -- one near Pensacola in Florida and another in Birmingham, Alabama.
AFP reporters saw overturned vehicles, downed trees and power lines, and numerous buildings with damaged roofs.
Streets along the coast were largely deserted after authorities ordered mandatory evacuations ahead of the storm.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis warned at a briefing Saturday afternoon that threats remained even though the storm had passed.
"Just be careful out there. Downed power lines, standing water, any of that can be very, very hazardous. Don't run any generators inside your home or inside your garage," he said.
The governor's warning came after a man was found dead in Florida earlier in the day with a generator running in his garage, CNN reported.
More than 500,000 US customers were without electricity Saturday night along the storm's path through Florida, Alabama and Georgia, according to the PowerOutage.com tracker.

The US energy department on Saturday authorized the release of up to four million barrels of reserve crude to stave off the impact of Isaias's path through the Gulf coast region, the country's oil refining hub.
Flood risks
A major flood threat remained as the storm headed northward and inland. The NHC warned that some areas could see upwards of 25cm of rain.
"Considerable flash flooding and landslides are also possible across the Southern Appalachians," it warned in a briefing.
The threat was particularly worrying in the mountains of North Carolina, where communities are still recovering from hurricane Helene of 2024.

That storm made landfall in the same Florida region as Isaias, but remained at tropical storm strength as it moved northward, dumping record amounts of rainfall into the mountains and leading to deadly flooding.
Isaias's late arrival this season is largely due to an El Nino of historic strength.
El Nino, the warm phase of the El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), creates strong vertical wind shear over the Atlantic that tends to tear storms apart.

"We have been seeing basically nearly record strong shear throughout the Atlantic Basin this year, and that is consistent with what we'd expect to see with a strong El Nino event," Michael Fischer, of the University of Miami's Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric, and Earth Science, told AFP.
In the Pacific, it has the opposite effect, weakening shear and allowing storms to grow. The Pacific has already produced several hurricanes this year, some of which hit maximum Category 5 strength.

Mexico's Baja California and the bordering US state of California were bracing for the landfall of Tropical Storm Rachel, expected late Saturday, as Hurricane Simon wreaked havoc along western Mexico.
38781b6b01f68521: A friend offered me a free ticket to the Bahrain Grand Prix at our very own Sepang International Circuit. I sadly declined. The crowd and the noise would have driven me crazy and it was best I stayed on my sofa watching the race on TV.
Here’s what I noticed afterwards: the single biggest type of comment on the many social media posts about it was: "Bring back F1 to Sepang!"

Malaysia hosted F1 races for 18 seasons until 2017. We watched Michael Schumacher, Lewis Hamilton, Sebastian Vettel, Fernando Alonso, etc., duke it out on one of the most beautiful motor racing circuits in the world. Then F1 went away.
It’s incredibly expensive to host F1 races with uncertain returns. At some point somebody did the numbers and pulled the plug. Sepang circuit went quiet, at least to Formula 1 races.

But its reputation remains. F1 aficionados looked forward to F1's return to Sepang. What I had thought were just irritations about Sepang, especially the afternoon rains, were actually what made races at Sepang unique, challenging and exciting.

Technically, the recent race was a Bahrain event hosted by Sepang after Bahrain cancelled their own event because of the war going on in that region. Their loss is our gain and now Bahrain as well as any of the other F1 hosts know that Sepang is always available to step in.

Being a last-minute host does bring about its share of problems. The crowd was huge – in excess of a quarter of a million people over the race weekend - and created massive issues with transport, safety, amenities, etc.

But such problems are unavoidable for such a late substitution, and they don’t detract from the race's success. That’s important because the race itself was amazing. The Sepang circuit lived up to its reputation, but other factors added to the drama.
The glitches in various software on the race cars as well as the rules around them caused by the rain will lead to major changes and Sepang will be remembered for that in F1 lore.

That so many people turned out over the long weekend surprised me. I had thought F1 had become passé and that the generation of us who like to hear cars that deafen us has been replaced by those who prefer the quiet swooshing of electric vehicles.

It seems the demise of petrol heads like us has been greatly exaggerated. There’s something captivating – perhaps a pleasure, perhaps a fear or perhaps both at once – in the ear-piercing shrieks of metal and rubber being propelled and piloted at ungodly speeds.

Not all of us old timers are old fossils whining about the demise of ICE (internal combustion engine) cars. The future is electric and F1 itself has been dipping its toes in it, even with the occasional hiccups we just saw.
Electric car racing will bring its own set of excitement when its time comes, and I'm sure Sepang will be ready for it.

For now, I’m happily basking in the reflected glory of Sepang’s success. Singapore’s own F1 race on its night-time street circuit is next, but I can guarantee that it’ll be judged less exciting than Sepang.

Singapore’s race is very much like Monaco’s – glitz, glamour and wealth with the vagaries of Sepang’s heat, humidity and rain added. It’s a finely-tuned race on streets that is not quite a free-for-all on a purpose-built circuit. There, you cannot hear the crowd’s roar over the cacophony when Lewis Hamilton brilliantly executes an overtaking manoeuvre.

At Sepang, Hamilton came third for a podium finish. Max Verstappen won this race, just as he won the very last race in Sepang in 2017. Fernando Alonso did well too. The old-timers are still around and kicking butt even in the much-maligned new F1 cars, rules, and technologies.

I’ve driven on the Sepang circuit in fancy German sports cars courtesy of another generosity. But high speeds freak me out and get my heart palpitating almost as fast as the engine’s revolutions. Brutal speed is not for me, and truth be told, I find rallying more exciting and freakish than F1.

But the world loves F1 more, and apparently loves Sepang very much too. Verstappen will certainly remember his victories here, especially his latest one. Sepang’s brilliant circuit plus the uncertainties of the weather – especially the heat and rain, and hopefully this time only, the haze – make it unique.

I wouldn’t be surprised if they bring F1 back to Sepang. If the economics work out, it would be an absolutely brilliant annual event for F1 lovers the world over and it’ll put Sepang closer to the rarified company of legendary F1 circuits past and present such as Monza, Silverstone, Spa-Francorchamps and Nürburgring.
I would be even less likely to attend, however, even if I were to become completely deaf, as my aversion to crowds wouldn’t change, and most likely would have increased.

But I’d enjoy it vicariously and derive great pleasure in hearing it described as one of the most exciting motor races in the F1 calendar, one held within a week of the race in Singapore where spectators and drivers go to relax and play go-karts over some streets for a few hours.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
29dc162276d9e77c: PETALING JAYA: At 5am, while most of the Taman Sri Manja neighbourhood is still asleep, Koong Poh Kang is already preparing for the day ahead.

His morning begins with charcoal, char siew and the familiar rhythm of getting a wantan mee stall ready for customers. The roasting alone takes about an hour and a half, but the work starts even earlier, with marination done the night before to give the char siew more flavour.
By 7am, the 25-year-old is ready to serve customers at Kang Kee Wan Tan Mee in Restoran Fai Wong - a business he decided to take over when he was just 23.
“I'm quite happy,” Koong said. “Every day there are different types of situations I have to deal with. But that's the fun part,” he said.

That happiness, however, comes with sacrifices. Koong has had to give up late nights out with friends, whose work schedules no longer match his own. Once his friends invited him to Genting Highlands in the middle of the night.
“I was quite upset because I couldn’t go,” he said. “I wished I could go, but I couldn’t because my work is really physically demanding.”
Eventually, he stopped dwelling on what he was missing. “After one year of me thinking about it, I was like, I'm just going to continue doing my thing.”
The decision to become a hawker came somewhat naturally to Koong. The second-oldest of five siblings, he helped his mother with her bak kut teh business during his primary school days.

In fact, becoming a hawker was his choice of career when his teacher asked his class what they wanted to be when they grew up. “I got laughed at,” he recalled. “At the time, I didn't really understand why.”

He eventually obtained an IT degree and worked a corporate job. But at 23, he began considering a different future when an opportunity came up: the owner of a wantan mee stall in his neighbourhood wanted to retire.

For Koong, it was an opportunity that combined familiarity with something he genuinely loved. “My favourite food as a child was wantan mee,” he said. “My parents used to bring us to this wantan mee stall in Old Klang Road. It was very good.”

Taking over the business still required him to prove that he could do the work. He spent six months learning from the previous owner without an income, picking up everything from preparing the ingredients to cooking the char siew.

FMT Lifestyle got to try Koong’s wantan mee, and honestly, this simple and humble dish hits all the nostalgic and culinary spots. The noodles are springy, the char siew sweet and tender, and the sauce is slightly peppery, making for a satisfying meal perfect for breakfast or lunch.

But there is a deeper reason Koong wanted to make the business work. Growing up, he watched his mother work hard to raise five children. She ran her bak kut teh business at the same kopitiam of his wantan mee stall for more than 10 years, and Koong remembers how stressful it was for her.
“I was like, okay, I'm going to help her retire as soon as possible,” he said. His mother has since moved from selling bak kut teh to selling pao, which Koong considers less demanding.

Ironically, although his workday starts much earlier than a typical office job, Koong now feels he has more time for himself. “After selling my wantan mee till 3pm, I have time to rest and go to the gym.”
Still, Koong is careful not to present his experience as a blueprint for other young people. His advice to those thinking of starting their own business is straightforward.
“Don't be so hasty,” he said. “You need to do a lot of research first.”
For Koong, knowing the neighbourhood, understanding its customers and having a personal connection to wantan mee gave him the confidence to take the leap.
At 25, he is now doing the job that once got him laughed at - and finding that there is more to being a hawker than he ever expected.

d21ae481f658436c: PETALING JAYA: The controversial littoral combat ship (LCS) project will still provide the navy with important and relevant assets despite repeated delays in the ships’ handover, say defence analysts.

While some quarters have suggested that the ships may be outdated by the time of delivery, defence analysts Lam Choong Wah and Salawati Mat Basir maintained that the LCS would still significantly enhance the Malaysian navy’s capabilities.
Lam, of Universiti Malaya, acknowledged that the ships’ management systems, situational awareness tools and weapons platforms may be lagging technologically by the time operations commence.
“However, by definition, this is not a ‘white elephant’ project that delivers nothing,” he said, adding that the LCS would still enhance our navy's capability significantly.
“So, it is still better than nothing,” he told FMT.

Salawati, a maritime affairs expert with Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia, said the LCS project was still critically needed by the navy. “Yes, it’s backwards to some extent, but we don’t have a choice.”

The LCS project, which had an original cost of RM9 billion, is said to be the largest defence procurement in Malaysia’s history. Delays and cost overruns have seen the cost balloon to RM11.22 billion, even as the number of vessels to be delivered has been cut from six to five.
The auditor-general’s report released on Oct 5 said the first LCS ship (LCS 1) might not be fully operational until December 2035, although defence minister Khaled Nordin disputed the projection.
The audit also found that, as of June 25, the overall LCS project was 7.55% behind schedule across all five ships, with delays ranging from 30 to 108 days.
Lam added to calls for a royal commission of inquiry (RCI) to investigate the troubled project, saying there were many sensitive documents that even the Public Accounts Committee could not access.
“Moreover, an RCI can recommend policy reform and pinpoint culprits,” he said.
Moving forward, he said, Malaysia’s defence procurement must be conducted with greater transparency and oversight, two elements that have been sorely absent for decades.

Lam said the issues that surfaced with the LCS were not an anomaly but a norm. While some may argue that defence procurements demand secrecy due to their sensitive nature, he said other nations have prioritised reforms for greater transparency and accountability.

Lam said a first step towards transparency would be listing out major defence procurements in the annual federal budget, while all procurements above RM100 million should automatically be placed under parliamentary oversight.
“Continuous oversight by the PAC, auditor-general and parliamentary committee on security must be automatically imposed on any defence procurement above RM100 million,” he said.

Salawati said the recurring issues in defence purchases were linked to the common practice of direct negotiations in the name of national security, allowing rigorous public and parliamentary scrutiny to be bypassed.

She called for a cross-service, cross-ministry procurement committee to oversee defence asset purchases, saying such a mechanism would ensure decisions were not left in the hands of a single individual.
“There should also be international open tenders, so that no one can take a cut from contracts,” she said.

fc3b064dc8ef63ad: From Jamaluddin Aziz

The sudden announcement by local film distributor Antenna Entertainments that A24’s psychological thriller "Primetime" has been banned by the Film Censorship Board (LPF) is more than a disappointment for film fans and scholars alike.
As a critical media studies scholar analysing our regulatory systems, I see this as a glaring case of policy misalignment that actively undermines the government’s own economic directives.
Once again, a high-profile international asset has been flatly erased from the local market without public justification.
Instead of treating these adjustments as routine protection, the government must evaluate how opaque decisions create structural risks that dismantle the industry.
If we expect our creative sectors to thrive globally, we must stop allowing unpredictable censorship to disrupt them from within.
Destabilising the Finas growth mandate
This enforcement strategy directly contradicts the developmental goals of the National Film Development Corporation Malaysia (Finas).

Just recently, Finas chairman Hans Isaac made a strong public case for increased national budget allocations to strengthen the local film ecosystem and elevate the global competitiveness of Malaysian stories.
The complete ban on "Primetime" represents a stark policy paradox that terrifies investors.
Instead of building a viable market, heavy-handed bans signal to international studios that the Malaysian theatrical space is highly volatile.
This regulatory uncertainty creates a chilling effect, forcing local filmmakers into defensive self-censorship out of fear their projects will be permanently shelved.
If the government wants a return on investment for public funds, it must first guarantee a stable environment where creative risks can safely exist.
Loss of public pedagogy and revenue

From an educational and media literacy standpoint, erasing complex texts like "Primetime", which critiques vigilante media and the sensationalism surrounding child exploitation, is deeply counterproductive.
Banning a film does not stop it from being consumed in the digital age. A theatrical ban simply drives audiences to illicit online spaces and foreign streaming platforms.
Instead of protecting the public, the government achieves zero educational oversight while local exhibitors and cinemas lose vital box-office revenue.
We are effectively routing taxable domestic entertainment expenditure straight out of the country, starving the exact ecosystem the communications ministry is trying to fund.
If we want citizens to develop critical thinking skills, we cannot keep removing the very educational materials required to teach them.
Need for structural transparency
We must move beyond treating film as mere passive entertainment.
Finas CEO Azmir Saifuddin Mutalib recently said that the censorship framework has shown signs of opening up by increasingly relying on age classifications like PG-18 over extensive cuts.
The banning of "Primetime" feels like a massive step backward from that progressive rhetoric.
Instead of systemic censorship that suffocates open discussion, LPF must transition toward a transparent classification system.
The board must publicly publish detailed, analytical justifications for its restrictions.
Explaining why a piece of content crosses cultural boundaries helps educate the public on media ethics and artistic boundaries, fostering a mature and responsible film culture.
If we trust Malaysians to vote, pay taxes, and raise families, we should at least trust them to sit in a dark room and critically analyse a movie.
Jamaluddin Aziz is an associate professor in critical media studies at Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia’s Centre for Research in Media and Communication and an FMT reader.

0c3a0aba01ce49de: We are told from childhood to heed traffic rules. Yet anyone who has driven on our roads knows that many of us treat them as suggestions, heeding them only when a policeman is visible at the junction. The moment we see that uniform, compliance becomes instantaneous.
We obey not because we have internalised the law’s moral force; we obey because we fear being caught.
This is not a peculiarity of Malaysian drivers — it is a reflection of human nature everywhere. And it applies just as much to the scourge of corruption.
People do not walk away from corrupt practices simply because they have learned to hate corruption or because it is a religious injunction. They stop because they fear being caught.
This observation exposes the limits of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s recent message to Gen Z.

Speaking at the National Student Figure Awards on Oct 1, 2026, he reminded undergraduates that a degree or a doctorate is no shield against greed. He noted that many of those implicated in major scandals such as 1MDB, Felda, and Tabung Haji are well educated.

His conclusion was sound: “A good education, therefore, does not make one virtuous.” But speeches are traffic signs — necessary, yet powerless without the policeman standing behind them. Advice, after all, is the easiest thing a politician can give.

Anwar also said he would be relentless in his pursuit of corrupt officials past and present, regardless of political fallout. Which means his rhetoric rests on two pillars: cultivating character in our young and pursuing corrupt officials.

Preaching to students costs nothing. It does not ask anyone in power to surrender their influence. Building a truly independent enforcement mechanism, however, is expensive, politically risky, and institutionally demanding.
Anwar should know this better than most. He spent decades on the outside arguing for these very structural changes. Now, he holds the keys to the house and he must build that policeman.

To be fair, the administration has taken formal steps, such as the establishment of the National Education Council and the National Education Blueprint 2026–2035, which aim to strengthen values and morals from primary school through higher learning.
This is a welcome bridge. But forming a council or launching a national plan is not the same as implementing deep reform.

Character education cannot remain trapped as slogans in civics textbooks. It requires teachers trained in moral reasoning rather than rote recitation; and it requires ethics to be treated with utmost seriousness in fields where misconduct carries the highest stakes — medicine, engineering, finance, and public administration.
Strengthening values in educational institutions will help the next generation and beyond. But a capable and independent policeman is needed at the junction today.

While the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) possesses the statutory power to initiate investigations independently, its structural vulnerability stems from executive oversight — chiefly that its leadership serves at the pleasure of the executive.

Reform advocates including G25 and Bersih have long urged that the MACC be removed from the Prime Minister’s Department and placed under parliamentary oversight via a constitutionally mandated independent anti-corruption commission.

But to be fair, the MACC under Anwar recorded 1,095 charges and 563 convictions from 2,633 investigation papers opened since 2024, with 583 involving high-profile and public-interest cases. Asset recovery has been aggressive: RM6.81 billion seized between January and August 2025 alone, against leakages estimated at RM277 billion over six years.
And three former prime ministers are among several top politicians facing trial.

Yet we see more cases of corruption emerging — Najib Razak’s discharge not amounting to an acquittal (DNAA) in his SRC International case (June 2025), ongoing probes into defence procurement and military officers, and Anwar’s public backing of MACC investigations into senior officials, the MACC 'corporate mafia' allegation — and we shake our heads saying corruption has become systemic.

Why? Is it that those handling public money are unafraid of being caught if they indulge in corruption? Is it because they feel they can get away if they are connected? Is it because givers feel they will get away with it? If this is so, enforcement needs to be tightened and those enforcing it must be of unquestionable integrity.

Do businessmen resort to bribes because they see it as the only way to ensure swift clearance of their problems or approvals for their initiatives by civil servants? If this is so, the systems and processes used by regulators need improvement.

Is corruption systemic because political parties are funded by monetary gifts from those who have gained government contracts? If so, the registrar of societies and the MACC need to scrutinise the accounts of all political parties to the minutest detail.

Also, there is the credibility question. Persistent structural bottlenecks — such as prosecutorial discretion resting solely with the attorney general — continue to fuel public perceptions of selective enforcement.

Hassan Abdul Karim, the admirable Pakatan Harapan MP for Pasir Gudang, told Parliament in January that government efforts were affected by public perception that corruption cases were being investigated inconsistently.
“From the outside, people see that some cases are investigated quickly, some are delayed, and sometimes cases are not investigated at all. Some cases lead to charges quickly, while others do not.”

Asking how the government could fully implement anti-corruption measures if elites and high-ranking national leaders received “discounts,” he said: “I am not saying this is a mistake, but something is not right. On one hand, we want to fight corruption fully, yet on the other, some are let off with ‘discounts’.”

“Moreover, among our elite leaders, both past and present, many court cases end with DNAA. Not only that, some are then given NFA (no further action). I sympathise with the officers of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission who diligently investigate these cases.”
No one can seriously argue against his points.

Civil society organisations such as Transparency International Malaysia have also reminded us that stagnant global perceptions reflect lingering anxieties over unresolved high-profile cases and controversial DNAA decisions.

Therefore, any move to make the MACC more effective and independent must be paired with the long-debated separation of powers between the attorney general (the government’s chief legal adviser) and the public prosecutor (who holds absolute constitutional discretion under Article 145(3) to institute, conduct, or discontinue criminal proceedings).
Although the government has agreed in principle to split these roles, the slow pace of constitutional amendments leaves a system where prosecutorial discretion remains tied to the executive.
This is the challenge facing the prime minister: he must willingly constrain his own power over the machinery of justice. And I don’t envy him.

As prime minister, Anwar holds the power to initiate and constitutionalise MACC independence, finalise the separation of the public prosecutor from the attorney general, reform public procurement and political financing, protect whistleblowers, ensure greater government transparency, and allow more freedom of expression.
Moral speeches set the tone; but the harder work is restructuring our systems so that corruption becomes difficult, risky, and socially unsustainable.
Our prime minister has told young Malaysians to hate corruption. He now has the historic opportunity to build the independent institutions that make wrongdoers fear it.

Just as we need the red lights and the visible policeman at the traffic junction to ensure full compliance, we need to complement advice and education in values with an effective and independent MACC and an autonomous prosecutor to put fear into potential wrongdoers and enforce the message that no one is above the law.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

c5abe7fc1e5d7868: For about a decade, the mainstream understanding has been that psychedelics cause chaos in the brain. Brain networks—the stable patterns of communication that handle vision, attention, or our sense of self, and more—loosen and start talking to each other all at once. EEG traces get noisier and more complex. “Think of the networks of the brain as highways,” says Devon Stoliker, a neuroscientist at Monash University. “Under psychedelics, these highways break down into many different directions.”

In a recent Nature study, Stoliker’s team designed an experiment to test whether these directions are truly chaotic and random. Researchers gathered 62 people who had never taken a psychedelic before, gave them 19 milligrams of psilocybin, a common psychedelic found in certain fungi, and scanned their brains. Then, they used AI to analyze the drugged and sober brain scans. What emerged was not exactly chaos.

Stoliker thinks chaos is not a satisfactory explanation for psychedelics’ effect on the brain. “It never really explained why an individual would have a meaningful experience, why they might have insight, why they might experience clarity, and why these might translate into positive psychological changes,” Stoliker says. To investigate if there are other explanations, he and his colleagues designed a study called PsiConnect.

4d9f8115982246d3: Researchers say two characters available to typosquatters and phisherfolk can trick Chromium browsers into displaying lookalike URLs as genuine web addresses. Wangling a domain name to look an awful lot like that of a popular website is nothing new. We’ve all encountered phishing sites such as macrosoft[.]com and applle[.]com before in our daily struggles against spam. However, as browsers mature, new characters are always being made available for use. This opens up new opportunities for those whose languages contain characters/homoglyphs that aren’t ASCII-compliant, but it also introduces new ways for attackers to abuse display logic quirks in programs like Chrome and Edge. According to Ian Muscat and Leanne Briffa of Have I Been Squatted, there are still characters available to cyber-imposters that can reliably fool web users into trusting URLs that they certainly should not. The latest glyphs bypassing browser safety checks allow tricksters to run websites from a clearly fake domain name (when displayed in Punycode), although they appear just like the real deal in Unicode. The characters of note, in this case, are ө, which is found in various Cyrillic languages such as Kazakh, Mongolian, and Tatar, and the Latin K with hook, ƙ, used in Hausa and Karai-karai. Both are visually similar to the letters e/o, i, and k, respectively, and allowed the researchers to register 20 lookalike domain names. These included: aррӏө[.]com sрасөх[.]com oƙta[.]com niƙe[.]com Below are the URLs’ Punycode equivalents – how browsers should display them safely: xn--80a6aa68c8d.com xn--80a5aeq0fr0c.com xn--ota-f6a.com xn--nie-g6a.com You can try them out; they’re registered by Have I Been Squatted and are safe to visit. They take you to research demo pages set up by the researchers, and each page explains how exactly they bypass browser protections. Crucially, they all bypass the key security measures deployed by Chromium-based browsers. How the bypasses work Browsers deploy two main defense layers. The first is a set of seven sequential checks run by Chromium’s SafeToDisplayAsUnicode function, which check for a range of common spoofing methods. Vendors began introducing these checks in 2017 after researcher Xudong Zheng registered аррӏе.com – a domain consisting of all-Cyrillic characters. Chromium’s checks, which factor in a hardcoded list of known Cyrillic characters known to be used in place of Latin letters, can be seen as "all or nothing." Built to detect all-Cyrillic strings, the measure only takes action against domain names if every character in the string is on its hardcoded list. If one character is missing, the check is bypassed. Characters such as ө, ї, and ү, are known as “breakers,” as these are not present in the lookalike list, as of Chrome 154 (released to stable channel on September 22). Failing any of the seven display checks tells the browser that the characters are unsafe to display as Unicode and to instead display the Punycode, revealing just how dissimilar they are to the genuine domains they try to imitate. The second measure browsers take is to compare the domain name against a list of popular websites to see if it is trying to imitate one of them. In Chromium, these checks are handled by the GetSimilarTopDomain() function. This step converts a supplied domain name into a "skeleton," stripping its characters of diacritics, such as accents (ó becomes o), and checking the skeleton URL against a hardcoded list of popular websites. Chromium checks against almost 8,500, and if the skeleton matches any of them, then it displays Punycode. However, the Latin K with hook, ƙ, does not have an accent, and is added to the skeleton as a Latin k with an added combining mark, bypassing the security check. In this case, the skeleton is formed as: [o k ‘ t a . c o r n]. (The skeleton maps "m" to "rn"). Likewise, with аррӏө.com, the Cyrillic barred o retains its bar in the skeleton as a combining mark, meaning it does not match the genuine Apple domain. Its skeleton is formed as: [a p p l o - . c o r n]. Browsers are always working to stymie these tools of imposterment. Chrome 148 put an end to attackers being able to use ҏ and ӿ as breakers to imitate their Latin lookalikes, for example. The two main security checks are not the only lines of defense. Chromium also deploys warnings at the time of navigation called Safety Tips. An example domain that would bypass the two main checks is ínstagarm[.]com. The inflection on the beginning character is removed and what’s left is essentially the real Instagram domain with two letters swapped. The Instagarm domain does not match any of the hardcoded sites, nor does it contain any banned characters. In this case, Chrome will display one of two popups, asking the user if they meant to visit the genuine domain, warning that the current direction of travel appears fake. However, there are limits to this extra security layer. The warnings only trigger when an imitation domain is an exact-character match, a one-edit match, or a match with an adjacent swap from the genuine URL. Two or more changes, like with аррӏө[.]com, which has all-Cyrillic characters preceding the ".com," will not trigger these warnings. The warnings will also not trigger with domains consisting of fewer than five characters. Domains such as oƙta.com, which is only one edit from the real Okta, may not trigger defenses because of the one-edit rule and the fact that it is only four characters. Safety Tips also checks the skeleton against the sites users visit regularly, not just the hardcoded list of trusted sites. Frequently visited sites may trigger the same warnings, but for users who do not have a comprehensive visit history, the defense layer may fail. The defenses described here only apply to browsers. Email clients are even less picky with imitation domain strings. Websites like Gmail displayed each of the 20 domains HIBS fed the clients, which were a mix of lookalikes and genuine internationalized domain names (IDNs), as an attacker would want it to, all in Unicode. Outlook Web showed all 20 as Punycode, even the harmless ones, suggesting neither apply the right checks to properly inform users. To quantify the scale of the issue, the researchers looked at ICANN’s list of every .com domain. There are around 167 million of them, approximately 733,000 of which are IDNs, those that contain non-ASCII characters and are stored in Punycode form. The researchers took each of the IDNs and swapped their non-ASCII characters for ASCII equivalents to determine how many matches there were. They found around 162,000 pairs – IDNs that resemble plain ASCII domains. It should be said that this does not mean there are circa 162,000 typosquatted domains, just that many yield lookalikes. Some may be registered by businesses for defensive purposes; others may be owned by the same business that wants to operate multiple websites catering to different languages. However, organizations should be aware of the means available to typosquatters, and monitor registered domains accordingly. ®

4fce54df6d7e0d56: You'd swear from the over-the-top reactions that someone is threatening to take European Commission workers' dogs out back and shoot them. Why the freakout? Because the EC is deploying a self-hosted alternative to Microsoft Teams to keep staff communicating if Microsoft's service becomes unavailable. To be clear, the Commission isn't replacing Teams with Element Pro; it's setting up a backup. That's it. That's all. But according to a Politico report, users are having fits. Element is "absolute shit," rants one. Another proclaims: "The US would 'instantly win the war' if it ever decided to switch off its technology." Uh, guy, that's exactly the point. If US providers cut off European users, whether by choice or government order, many EU governments and companies would face serious disruption. That's exactly why Europe needs an open source, sovereign backup. That's the entire point of this exercise. Take away all the hysteria, and you're left with a rather mundane business-continuity initiative. Don't think for a minute that Trump wouldn't have a snit and order tech giants to block services to officials. Just ask Kimberly Prost, a Canadian International Criminal Court judge, who, besides losing tech services, also lost her credit cards, access to Amazon and Google services. "Alexa wouldn't talk to me," she says – punishment indeed. Now imagine Russia and its allies start attacking the Baltic states. Oh, wait, Putin is already doing that. Then it gets heated, and Trump decides to side with his good friend Putin. What happens to American tech companies' services in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania? I can answer that in two words: "Nothing good." That said, the EC of course is not dumping Microsoft services. No, it has configured Element Pro to run on the Commission's own infrastructure. An internal memo described the service as an "internal backup" that gives the EU's executive branch an alternative channel for internal messaging, audio and video calls, file transfers, and project discussion rooms. Let me spell it out for you. This is a Commission initiative. It's not an EU-wide order to abandon Microsoft software. I'd love that myself, but that's not what's happening here. Teams will remain the principal platform, while Element provides a fallback intended to reduce dependence on an externally operated communications service. Got it? I hope so! Mind you, there are other good reasons to dump Microsoft Teams. I'm not a fan. For my sins I have to use it and every other groupware program out there. And, I might add, I've been using them since Lotus Notes rolled out the door in 1990. Digital sovereignty isn't just a good idea. It's essential. Or, as an EC July staff memo put it: "In practice, this means having greater control over our data and systems so that we can reduce risks and limit disruption to our work, wherever possible." Exactly so. Element's architecture is well suited to digital sovereignty. Built on Matrix, an open standard for real-time communications, the platform supports self-hosting, decentralized operation, and interoperability with other Matrix-based systems. Element also supports end-to-end encrypted messaging and calls. You see, the sovereignty argument isn't just about getting an EU-based technology stack. After all, Element is a British company. No, what really makes Element a winner for the EC is that it's mature groupware that lets them deploy and run the system on their own infrastructure rather than relying on Microsoft's cloud. As for the crybaby users, suck it up. No one ever likes change. If the EC switches over to Element lock, stock, and barrel, I suspect much of today's outrage will be forgotten in six months. From what we see in the field, open source alternatives like Element are ready for primetime as a much needed alternative to dependency on the big tech vendors."

1705d980b8a49d70: Nearly a third of developers who use AI daily spend four hours or more of their working day with it, according to Stack Overflow's latest survey. The survey received 30,903 responses from developers and technologists across 169 countries. Among the 10,926 daily AI users who answered the time-use question, about 80 percent reported using the tools for at least an hour a day. The research by developer Q&A site Stack Overflow also found skepticism from developers toward using AI in their roles. Only about 7 percent of developers said they trusted AI output for important work decisions, while 48 percent trusted it when they could easily verify the output. Seventy-nine percent considered source attribution important or very important when deciding whether to trust an AI-generated technical answer. Stack Overflow CEO Prashanth Chandrasekar said developers were highly skeptical as a group. "As AI agents become rapidly more autonomous, that skepticism now acts as a critical safeguard. Trust is not a given when it comes to developers; it is earned through transparency, source attribution, and rich technical context." The survey found that coding assistants or coding agents are used by 66 percent of respondents, general-purpose chat tools by 63 percent, and automated agent workflows by 26 percent. Seventeen percent of respondents said they did not use AI tools. Stack Overflow's commercial relationships with AI companies have proved contentious. 6c3986e9c32847be: From Saarani Vengadesen
Malaysia talks increasingly about becoming a high-income, knowledge-based economy. We talk about artificial intelligence, digitalisation, advanced manufacturing and jobs of the future.
But there is another group of young Malaysians whose future deserves more attention: our life sciences graduates.
I often hear that Malaysia is lacking life sciences graduates.
As a biotechnology graduate, I find that statement difficult to reconcile with my own experience and with the experiences of many graduates I have encountered.

Malaysia has universities offering biotechnology, microbiology, biochemistry, molecular biology, genetics, food science and other life sciences programmes. Every year, students graduate from these courses hoping to build careers in science.

Yet many soon discover that finding a job directly related to their degree is not straightforward. So, do we really lack life sciences graduates, or do we lack life sciences jobs? There is an important difference.

Malaysia has invested in biotechnology and the bioeconomy for years. We have national policies, research institutions, universities and programmes designed to develop the sector. We continue to encourage young people to pursue science and technology.
But somewhere between graduating from university and entering the workforce, the pathway becomes unclear.

This is not because life sciences are becoming less relevant. Quite the opposite. The world is entering an era where biology is increasingly central to how we address major challenges, from food security and climate change to new medicines, sustainable materials and agricultural innovation.
The question is whether Malaysia is creating enough opportunities for the people trained to work in these fields.
For too many graduates, the options appear to be limited: remain in academia, compete for a small number of research positions, continue studying or take a job outside their field.
We often respond by saying that graduates need to become more “industry-ready.”
But perhaps we should also ask whether the industry is ready to absorb the talent our universities are producing.
A life sciences career should not mean spending an entire career at a laboratory bench or leaving the field altogether.

The modern life sciences sector needs people who understand science and can work across disciplines. There are careers in regulatory affairs, biosafety and biosecurity, science communication, intellectual property, technology transfer, clinical research, agricultural policy, food systems, environmental management, business development and science and technology governance.
These pathways exist, but they are rarely visible to students.
Malaysia also needs to look beyond producing graduates and start thinking about building a life sciences workforce.

We need better data on where life sciences graduates go after university. We need stronger university-industry partnerships, meaningful internships, industry-linked curricula and clearer pathways from research to employment.
Most importantly, we need to create and attract companies and institutions that can provide meaningful careers for this talent.
Research cannot remain trapped in laboratories and universities.
A discovery only creates wider value when it moves through the ecosystem from research to innovation, regulation, investment, commercialisation and ultimately society.
Our life sciences graduates should be part of that entire journey.
Malaysia has invested significantly in building its scientific and biotechnology capabilities. We should not allow the people trained to sustain that ecosystem to become an afterthought.
The future of work is changing rapidly. Our graduates will need interdisciplinary skills, digital literacy and the ability to work across science, technology, policy and society.
But they also need something equally important: an economy that has a place for their expertise.
If we want Malaysia to be a knowledge economy, we cannot only ask our young people to acquire the skills of the future.
We must also build the future in which those skills are needed.
Saarani Vengadesen is CEO and founder of Orbis Policy Consulting.

e1f19a014ba94a30: Microsoft has joined the Jev fan club, an accidental group of companies that share a common desire to be recognized for their own decision models. Jev, announced by TypeSafe AI three weeks ago, is a large language model (LLM) tuned to respond to certain types of questions with a limited range of responses, rated by probability. Due to its speed, relative affordability, and response constraints, it's well-suited for a variety of business applications where open-ended text of uncertain accuracy might be undesirable. One of the selling points of Jev is that decision models don't hallucinate in the way that standard LLMs do. But decision models can make errors and their popularity has already prompted researchers to explore how those errors might be magnified. Nonetheless, they have their uses. The attention lavished on Jev prompted other companies to declare that they too have decision models to offer, even though machine learning researchers have long been able to create classifier models for probability-based decisions. OpenAI said its Decisions API has entered public beta. Cloudflare chimed in with its Clef model. Strands trotted out Strands Decider 2B, "a small, open source, decision model." Liquid AI introduced d1. Perplexity launched its Decisions API. Snowflake talked up its own decision model. Then there's Surogate Rune and H2O.ai's H2O-Lightning-4B, a decision model built on Qwen3.5-4B. All told, more than 100 such models are now vying for attention. Now it's Microsoft's turn. "Decision models are quickly emerging as an important new category in AI," said Achint Srivastava, VP of software engineering in the Office of the CTO at Microsoft, in a blog post on Friday. "Unlike LLMs, which are designed to generate text or reason through complex problems, decision models are purpose-built to deliver structured outputs that software can immediately act on. And once you understand that capability – making decisions and classifying things at very low cost with high performance – all kinds of useful tasks get unlocked." Microsoft's entrant into the race is called Microsoft-Decision-1, which is offered via Microsoft Foundry and, soon, via OpenRouter. Redmond's decision model, like H2O's, is based on a Qwen model, Qwen3.5-9B in this instance. The Qwen model family is developed by Alibaba Cloud, the cloud computing arm of Chinese tech giant Alibaba. Microsoft, for reasons not disclosed, said it will soon rebase the Decision-1 on its models and those from OpenAI. The US software giant claims its model is 2.5x faster than H2O-Lightning-4B and 2.8x faster than Jev in its latency test, leads the pack in accuracy (83.5 percent) on 36 benchmarks, ranks second (behind Quyet-1.0-Large) in confidence score (92.2 percent), and is more than 20x cheaper than OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol in text classification tasks. Input tokens cost $0.042 per million tokens and output tokens are free. "Now that agentic AI is a reality, we’ve seen that cost plays a major role in how people decide to use AI," said Srivastava. "And it’s increasingly important to choose the right model for the right job." ®
